About: Motion in a Potential — Bound, Free, or Balanced on the Edge

Source

Lecture
Classical mechanics — energy methods: 1-D motion in a potential landscape V(x)
Simulation
"Motion in a Potential — Bound, Free, or Balanced on the Edge" — energy-diagram mode with a ✓/⚠ counterfactual pair of speed rules
Concept
The height of the total-energy line E relative to the barrier top Vb — not the local slope — decides the fate of the motion: bound oscillation (E < Vb), escape (E > Vb), or the separatrix (E = Vb), where the time to reach the unstable maximum diverges.
Serves
Reading energy diagrams: allowed region, turning points where V(x)=E, KE = E − V(x); classifying equilibria via V″ (stable minimum at x = +1 m, unstable maximum at x = −1 m, barrier Vb = ⅔·s = 0.6667 J at s = 1); critical slowing on the separatrix.
Inquiry
Where along the track is the ball fastest? What changes as E crosses Vb? With E = Vb exactly, does the ball ever arrive at the top?
Misconception
"The ball's speed at a point is set by how steep the potential is there." Slope sets ACCELERATION a = −V′(x)/m; SPEED is set by E − V(x) — fastest at the minimum, zero at turning points.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Meet the energy diagram

The curve is V(x) = s(x³/3 − x). The cyan dashed line is total energy E; the amber dashes mark the barrier top Vb at x = −1 m. With E below Vb, the ball is trapped in the right-hand valley — released from rest at x₀ ≈ 1.8 m.

2 · Predict — where is it fastest?

Once released in this bound well, where along the track is the ball moving fastest?

3 · Watch the energy budget

Press ▶ Play if needed. Trail dots space out widest at the bottom; v → 0 at the turning points where V(x) = E. Compare the cyan v-arrow with the magenta a-arrow: at x = +1 m, a = 0 while v peaks.

4 · Predict — raising E past Vb

The amber line is the barrier height. If you raise E above Vb, what happens to the ball?

5 · Escape, then the separatrix

E is now above Vb — watch the one-pass escape. Then try Snap E = Vb (separatrix): the ball creeps toward x = −1 m but never arrives — the gap halves every t½ = 0.49 s — forever. That critical energy is the separatrix.

6 · Slope sets a — energy sets v

⚠ Slope sets speed is on: v ∝ |V′|, energy ignored. It stalls at the flat bottom (where the real ball is fastest), never turns, and ignores E. Flip back to ✓ Energy sets speed — height of E vs V(x) decides both speed and fate.

The landscape and its equilibria
Equilibria where V′ = 0: x = ±1 m. V″(+1 m) = +2s > 0 → stable minimum, V(+1) = −⅔s. V″(−1 m) = −2s < 0 → unstable maximum, barrier Vb = V(−1) = ⅔s (= 0.6667 J at s = 1).
Speed from energy — not from slope
v is set by the gap E − V(x): maximal at the minimum, zero at turning points where V(x) = E. The slope only sets the acceleration a(x) = −V′(x)/m.
The separatrix: time to the top diverges
Linearized near the top (ξ = x + 1) at E = Vb: exponential approach with rate λ = √(2s/m); each halving of the gap costs t½ = ln2/λ. The ball approaches forever — it never arrives.
The ⚠ counterfactual rule (for contrast)
The tested (wrong) rule: speed ∝ steepness, calibration τ = 1 s. It predicts stalling at BOTH x = ±1 m and no dependence on E — contradicted by the observed maximum speed at x = +1 m.

The Physics

Motion in a Potential — Bound, Free, or Balanced on the Edge · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A ball rides along a hilly landscape described by its potential energy V(x), and a cyan line marks its total energy E. The sim shows where the ball is allowed to go for a chosen E, and how it moves there.

What you'll learn

  • How to read an energy diagram: V(x), the line E, and the gap between them.
  • How the speed at a point follows from E and V(x).
  • How the two flat points of the curve differ.
  • How the position of the E line relative to the curve limits where the ball can be.
The landscape V(x), the energy line E, the barrier line Vb and the ball at its release point.

What's on screen

  • The curve V(x) = s(x³/3 − x), with a valley on the right and a hilltop on the left.
  • Dashed E line: the ball's total energy. The amber dashed line is the barrier Vb, the height of the hilltop.
  • The ball with a fading trail of dots, and white dots on the E line where V(x) = E.
  • Arrows: cyan for the velocity, magenta for the acceleration. They appear once the ball is running.
  • Chips at the top left name the regime and give the speed.
See itPress Play and watch the ball move along the curve. Watch for: the ball moving along the curve under the dashed E line, with a trail of dots behind it.

03

Energy sets the speed, the slope sets the acceleration

The total energy is kinetic plus potential, and it stays fixed as the ball moves:

E = ½mv² + V(x)  ⇒  v = √(2[E − V(x)] / m)
E − V(x) is the kinetic energy at x.

So the speed at a point depends on the gap between the E line and the curve there. It is largest where the gap is largest, and zero where the curve meets the line.

The slope does a different job. The force is −V′(x), so the acceleration is a = −V′(x)/m. It says how fast v is changing, not how large v is. At x = +1 m the slope is zero, yet the opening settings give the top speed there: v = √(2 × (0.30 + 0.667)) = 1.390 m/s. At the release point x₀ = 1.8 m the ball has v = 0.559 m/s and a = −2.24 m/s².

See itPress Play with the opening settings. Watch for: the cyan v arrow longest as the ball crosses the valley floor at x = +1 m, where the magenta a arrow shrinks away; the readouts reach about 1.39 m/s there.
04

Turning points mark the edge of the allowed region

Kinetic energy cannot be negative, so the ball can only be where E − V(x) ≥ 0. The ends of that region are the turning points, where V(x) = E. There v = 0 and the force turns the ball back.

  • For E = 0.30 J the turning points are x = −0.310 m and x = 1.866 m, so the ball shuttles between them. One round trip takes about 5.3 s.
  • Lower E and the region shrinks toward the valley floor. At E = Vmin = −0.667 J the ball just sits at x = +1 m.

The release point x₀ only chooses the starting spot. The ball starts moving toward −x with the speed E allows there, so it starts from rest only when x₀ is a turning point. If x₀ lies outside the allowed region, the sim moves it to the nearest allowed point.

See itPress Play with E = 0.30 J. Watch for: two white dots labelled v = 0 on the E line, and the Turning pts readout showing −0.310, 1.866 m.
05

Equilibrium points: a valley is stable, a hilltop is not

At an equilibrium the force is zero, so V′(x) = s(x² − 1) = 0 and x = ±1 m. The sign of V″(x) = 2sx tells the two apart.

xV″Vkind
+1 m+2s−2s/3 = −0.667 Jstable minimum
−1 m−2s+2s/3 = +0.667 Junstable maximum

Nudge the ball off the valley floor and the force points back toward it. Nudge it off the hilltop and the force points away. The barrier Vb is the value of V at the hilltop, 2s/3, so it grows with the potential scale.

With E just above Vmin the ball rocks about x = +1 m, with a period near 2π√(m/2s) = 4.44 s.

See itPress Play with E = −0.60 J. Watch for: the ball rocking to and fro about the green dot at x = +1 m, between the turning points 0.729 and 1.248 m.
06

Escape depends on E compared with the barrier

With E below Vb the curve rises above the E line on both sides of the valley, so the ball is trapped. Raise E above Vb and the left turning point disappears: the allowed region now runs on to x → −∞.

Below Vb there are two turning points. Above it there is only one, on the right.

The ball then crosses x = −1 m still moving, at v = √(2[E − Vb]/m), and does not come back. For E = 1.25 Vb = 0.833 J that speed is 0.577 m/s. The scale s moves the barrier: the same E = 0.30 J is trapped at s = 1 but escapes at s = 0.4, where Vb = 0.267 J.

See itChoose E above Vb and press Play. Watch for: the ball passing x = −1 m and running off to the left, with the chip reading ESCAPED.
See itSet the potential scale to s = 0.4 with E = 0.30 J. Watch for: the amber barrier line dropping below the E line, and the ball escaping.
07

The separatrix is the borderline between trapped and escaping

If E equals Vb exactly, the left turning point sits on the hilltop at x = −1 m. Near it, with ξ = x + 1, the gap is E − V = s ξ² (2 − x)/3 ≈ s ξ². So v = λξ with λ = √(2s/m), and the distance to the top shrinks exponentially:

ξ = ξ₀ e−λt,   t½ = ln 2 / λ = 0.490 s
Half-time of the approach at s = 1 and m = 1 kg.

The gap halves every 0.49 s but never reaches zero, so the ball needs infinite time to arrive. A little less energy and it turns back; a little more and it crosses. At s = 2 the half-time drops to 0.347 s.

See itChoose Snap E = Vb and press Play. Watch for: the ball slowing as it nears x = −1 m without arriving, the chip reading ON THE EDGE, and the Turning pts readout showing −1 (t→∞).
08

Where it matters

  • Pendulum. The bob hanging straight down is the stable minimum of its potential energy, and balanced upright is the unstable maximum. With just enough energy to reach the top, it takes forever to arrive, as on the separatrix.
  • Molecules. The potential energy of two bonded atoms has a minimum at the bond length. Below the energy of the separated atoms they vibrate about it; above it they fly apart. Real bond curves level off instead of falling forever.
  • Where it stops working. With friction, E is not constant: a ball in the valley loses energy and settles at x = +1 m. The method also needs the force to depend on position only.
09

Summary

In one line. An energy diagram shows where a ball can be and how fast it moves, once the energy E is chosen.

Key points

  • v = √(2[E − V(x)]/m) and a = −V′(x)/m.
  • Equilibria are where V′ = 0: stable if V″ > 0, unstable if V″ < 0.
  • Turning points are where V(x) = E. E = Vb is the borderline case.

Common mix-ups

  • "The ball is fastest where the track is steepest." Steepness gives the acceleration. The speed comes from E − V(x).
  • "The ball must stop at the top of a barrier." With E above Vb it still has kinetic energy there and carries on.
  • "At E = Vb the ball reaches the top and stays." It gets ever closer and never arrives.

Things to try on your own

  • Open the Measurements panel and check the speed at x = +1 m against √(2[E − Vmin]).
  • Find the smallest E that escapes at s = 1, then at s = 2, and compare with 2s/3.
  • Snap E = Vb and use Speed 0.25× to time how long v takes to halve.
